blocks.x: How you might give your name Mr. Dawson?
Eddie Dawson.
Any middle name? Eddie Joseph Dawson.
That's good.
I'll ask a couple questions, see like where you were born right here in New Orleans.

I started the playing in 1904 at Hugh Cloth's Dance Hall with O'Neill Lavish's Band, Franklin Y. Iberville. 1905 at Tom Anderson with Moran's Band, Basin and Iberville. 1907 at Harry Parker's Dance Hall, Dawson and Minetta's Band, Franklin between Iberville and Benwood. 1910 at Biller Phillips Dance Hall, Cornelius Jackson's Band, Franklin near Iberville. 1912 Liberty near Iberville, Huntson Nagel's Dance Hall with Joe Oliver's Band. 1915 with Chris Kelly's Band. 1918 Kid René's Band. 1921 Pippa Light Charles Band.
192 D&P Church
As he said, he went there at 4. 1904. He lived. At Puclos.
At Puclos there, 1904.
I thought it was 4 when we were at Parker's. At Parker's.

Well, it could have been 1903 at Puclos. I'm just, it's just about, I can't exactly remember. But I think that's about near as it could be. I'd say we started at Puclos in 1903. Then we started at Harry Parker's in 1940. And we worked at Harry Parker's for about 3 or 4 years. And then, when I left there, I went to Tom Anderson's at the Moran's band. Then at 1910, with Bill Phillips, Dan's called, and he is Jackson's band.
I was going to ask some more about that very first band you played in at Puclos. Who else was in the band, the leader and all?
The O'Neil Lavish here, a violin player. And, let's see. And what did you play, by the way? I was playing the tenor banjo. Tenor banjo.
Yeah, tenor banjo. And, uh, saxophone and trumpet. And he was just a small group of strings?
Only a small band of five pieces. And there were three other bands we had there playing with us. I can't remember them just now. You remember the other instruments?
You say there was a—
We had piano, we had violin, and tenor banjo, and saxophone and trumpet.

Did you use the saxophone there, or was it a clarinet? No, a saxophone. I was going to ask some more when you started in music. If you don't mind even telling when you were born, what was your birth date? 84. 24th of July. And, uh, exactly? 24th of July. 24th of July. And, uh, I wondered if your parents played any musical instrument? None at all. Or did you have any brothers and sisters, anybody else in the family, or uncles that played?
No, no relatives. No relatives at all.
Played music. No. How did you get interested in music?
How come you didn't get that music? I just picked it up from a kid. It was in me. Yeah.
What was your first instrument?

Uh, guitar. Did you have lessons on that, or did you pick it up yourself? Yeah, I just picked it up myself. Just picked up a guitar and tuned it up myself without anybody showing me. Really? Cool. How old were you about when you got it? I was about 20, 19 or 20 years old.
You weren't a real little kid then, then you didn't. Fast start running your little boy. Oh yeah.
Um. No, I did play with Kid Clayton.
This spot job, Kid Clayton, he was happy pounds.
Oh yes.

Yes, we know that. I had, I got a cut. That's all lately though. Oh that's, that's lately. Well that's about, say around about, about seven, eight years ago now. I was interested in that very early times too.
See this is one of the pictures that I have.

I don't have the whole band, but I do have a few of us with the good kids, you see. Let's see, is this the seminar? That's the seminar? That's the Oakland And this is Clayton over the trumpet. This is me with the bass.
The drummer looks like it could be Giles.
Let's see. No, that was Jock. Oh, yeah. I'll in Jock. Yeah, I remember. Yeah, Jock. He's way in the background. I couldn't see.
Yeah, Jock.
One more I didn't see underneath.
This is right. They're all the same. They're all the same. Yeah, Kit Clayton and his happy pals.
Where was this taken?
That was taken at a private dance. Oh, yeah. Uptown.

I was going to ask a little bit more. I don't want to bother you a lot of questions, but I wondered when you were a boy, who the bands were you heard when you were a boy, even before you took up music?

Were there any brass bands or parades or dance bands you remember? No. Yeah, yeah. Most of the time was just string instruments, see? And, well, of all the bands I played with was full bands. Yes. I mean, even before you took up music, do you remember going to any dances or hearing any music? Oh, yes. I used to go to dances. Do you remember which bands you played? Well, practically most all they had the Blazer Way band. They had the Charlie Galloway's band. And they had the Silver Leaf band. Yeah. They used to have lawns. And they had the Oliva band. Yeah. They used to have lawns. Every week they had a lawn party up there. What was this band? And they had the Olivia band. Yeah. They used to have lawns every week. They'd have a lawn party up there.
What was this band? Ms. Cole, Ms. Cole's lawn garden up there on Magnolia Street. You mentioned, was that called Blaze Away band? What was that? I never heard of that before.
Yeah, that was a Creole band from downtown. Do you remember anybody in that band? No.
Did they have some of the blowing instruments too or mostly strings?

They had blowing instruments too, yeah. Oh, the dance band? Yeah, they had, I think Bunk Johnson was playing in one of the bands at that time. Remember Bunk Johnson? Bunk Johnson was playing with the Silver Leaf, I think. Well, I played with the Silver Leaf for a good while. There's spot jobs, you know, up on the Pelican. Who was the leader of that? Uh, uh, Poisey Umphrey. Oh, Percy or was it his father? No, Poisey. Poisey, yeah. Poisey Umphrey. Willie Umphrey. Willie Umphrey. Willie Umphrey, yeah. The clarinet player. Yeah. Because his father, his name was Willie Umphrey too, but the old man, he was playing saxophone and clarinet. He played with us at Harry Parkers before we got George Backhead. How was? After Billy Phillips caught on fire, that's when they were going down. You know, well, I was playing with them then and we left to play a special job over the rhythm. And we didn't know nothing about it. When we come back, Billy Phillips' place was going down. Oh, no. So that's why then I left and went with you all.
Was that the place called, um, later the Entertainers or 101 Ranch? Yeah.
It was the, uh, 101, uh, the, uh, 101 Ranch place. And after. And after. And then in the tennis. Mm-hmm.
Um, I was going to ask some more about, um, if you ever had any teacher at all, after you took up the instrument a while, if you took lessons on the, uh, guitar?

No, I had a, I had a white, uh, fellow that gave me a few lessons, but he was, uh, with, uh, off from circuit. He came here and he stayed about a month. I take about four lessons from him and he had to go away then. Remember his name? No. He didn't get his name. I remember. He just gave me, he just showed me the fingerboard of the instrument, you know, and told me what kind of method to get, you see. And with the aid of Mr. Fess Mineta, I learned a whole lot. Thank you a lot. Thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you. When did you take up the, uh, tenor banjo? I take it right up after I put the guitar down. Take up the tenor banjo and, uh, uh, How long have you played guitar about? I played guitar about six or seven years.
Uh, Sunday night over at the Greenough, you mentioned that you'd played with Robichaux

before. I played with John Robichaux's band, the old man Robichaux, yeah. I played guitar with him at the Lyric Theater. But I, I don't think I stayed with him over a year. Right after I left, he got Kutche Martin on the guitar. Then after he, Kutche Martin stayed with him about a year or so. Then he got Bud Scott. And they went, they, uh, they was playing jobs, spot jobs, all out in the pool and building all out throughout the country. And then Bud Scott stayed with him until the band went down.

Uh, I know it's difficult to remember exact dates all the time. I don't like to bother you with all those dates. But do you know about when that would be? Was it before the First World War or after? Oh, yeah. Real early?
Before the First World War. Yes. Oh, yeah.
The Lyric Theater was running way back in there.

Oh, yeah, yeah. I didn't know how early the theater ran. Yeah, they had a full band at the Lyric Theater. Yeah. John Robichaux said that he had a full band there. Okay. I remember. You don't know the exact year. I remember.
Can you remember about what year? No, let's see.
That was some way around. Yeah, that was built up in around about 1908.
Before you played with Billy Phillips Dancehall. Yeah, that was one. Yeah. And you were playing guitar in those days. Guitar, yeah. Then you changed the tenor band.

Tenor band, yeah. When did you take up the bass? I had taken up the bass after I put the tenor band on. I had taken up the bass. They hired me, what you call, Emmanuel Perez, them. They had some misunderstanding with Billy Moran, the bass player. Yes. And they led Billy Moran. It was Imperial Band. Huh? It was Imperial. Imperial Band. They hired me and I stayed with them.
Did you have any lessons on the string bass or did you pick that up?
No, I didn't have no. I just picked it up.
Well, how long were you on that? Did you play that tenor band, Joe, I think?
Yes. Well, I did get the lesson from the young man showed me from the office. He gave me about four lessons on the tenor banjo. He gave me the fingerboard.
And how many years did you play the tenor banjo?
Oh, I played that tenor banjo ten years or so.

Ten years. Ten years. You played that quite a while. Yeah. The other night you mentioned the first time that Freddie Peppard came by and played with you. Was that at Parker's? Can you tell us about that again?

No, that was at the 101 Ranch. We only had string instruments there. And first Minetta was on the piano, then John Bean was on the drum. Old man Bean, Tarcum, on the drum. And I was playing the guitar then. Wasn't I playing? Yeah, I was playing the guitar then. And then we had the old man Willie O'Pri on the clarinet, sax. And we didn't have nothing. We had Jimmy Pala on the violin. Jimmy Pala. I got Jimmy for you. Yeah, you got Jimmy for you.

And then after, a little running come in. Yeah. Old man officer got a running and he had the boys, what they call him, he packs up his instrument. The gold's art. And you went behind and crossed the 25 and that was old John. That was George. That guy right.
To take him in there.
George.

And then, yes that's right. Now then they, then after we got Freddie, Freddie came in from a job. He played a job on his trunk. Well they wasn't, they didn't have, they didn't allow no blowing instruments.
It was against the law, was it?

It was against the law to blow brass instruments in the district. So, uh, Harry Parker asked me what instrument was that and I told him a trumpet. So he said, well tell him to play something. And he said, oh boss I can't play nothing, it's a violation of the law. I'm afraid, but if you protect me, I'll play. He said, well I'll, I'll protect you. He said, go ahead, there ain't nobody gonna do you nothing. So he blowed his trumpet and right after that he asked, it sounds so good he asked me, do you think you can get that fella to play a regular? I said, well I'll, he said, I'll go see the mayor and get a permit. I believe you told us the other night that all the women came from the, her birthday women. Yeah, all, that was at the, at Ponson Nagels. Was that across the street or? No, the next block at Liberty, Liberty in, in, in, uh, And they heard Freddie playing. And they heard the band of Freddie was playing the trumpet that, that drawed all of them over there because they had never heard a trumpet, you see. And, uh, well then after Harry Parker went to the mayor and got a permit to have, to have a blowing instrument, that made the Huntson Nagel then go hard your arms up there, you see. Full band, the Magnolia band, that was the name of the band at that time. Well he had a full band, about six or seven pieces then.
Previously that was all string band.
Mm-hmm.
But, uh, pardon me. But your first line up was when I knew you. Behind me was Black Pete's person. Who? Black Pete. Black Pete.
Black Pete, you see the piano player? Yeah.

I played the piano one, she. Yeah. In your head, uh, you was playing the guitar. Yeah. And, uh, you had, uh, Joe Nicklaus playing that. Yeah. That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right.
Yeah. That's right. Yeah.
And, uh, first, uh, music. Yeah. And after, made a change, uh, that's where you got, uh, old men in Oakland. Oh, yeah.

And, uh, uh, uh, Jimmy. Jimmy Palau. Yeah. Oh, man. Dean on, on the drum. Yeah, John Bill. And, uh, we, we, we only had, uh, uh, uh, clarinet and piano and guitar and drums. We didn't have, uh, we didn't have no, uh, blowing instruments at all outside of the breed. That's all.
Yeah. And, uh, I first knew you. That's why I first knew a father called Joe Nicklaus.
Yeah. Well, Joe Nicklaus played clarinet. He played clarinet. Yeah. Then after we got old man on for it then. And after Joe left, got old man on for it. Then we got, uh, George Beckman. Yeah.

And, uh, taking Jimmy in. I got Jimmy in for you. It was all gonna feel like. Oh, yeah. I got Jimmy in for you. George was jamming around 25. Yeah. Went up, going out that night. That's right. Taking George. That's right? Yeah, that's right. That's right.

Jimmy, uh, Palau, I think? Yeah, Palau. Mm-hmm. And, uh, most of them fellas is all dead now. Oh, yeah. I wonder if you can tell us about the King Oliver. Is he remembering when you first heard him play? And when you worked with him and all about him?

When, uh, Oliver, Joe Oliver, when I first got Joe Oliver, he only could play brass band music. He couldn't play no dance music. He had a, he had a, uh, a shoe shop uptown repairing shoes. Joe did that? Joe Oliver. He didn't know any of them. Yeah, and I, I went to hire him to play a dance up on St. Charles Street with me. I had the job and he told me that, uh, uh, he wasn't able to play no dance music. But he would get me somebody called, uh, John Peniton, I think it is. He was a trombone player, but he couldn't play. No. John Peniton was a trumpet player. Trumpet, but he played trumpet. Yeah, but he, he was some kind of trombone player too, so. No, John Peniton, he played trumpet player.
Yeah. But sometime he would play in the brass band, he played baritone. Yeah.

So anyhow, he, he, he recommended him to me and I got him and he played the job. Yeah. Now Joe Oliver didn't, couldn't play no brass band music. I mean, no dance music. No dance. No dance music, but he played brass band music. And right after that, Joe Oliver began to pick up the dance music. Next thing I heard, he was able to play. That's when he went and worked Butler.
Mm-hmm. Waked out on, uh, uh, uh, town on the big avenue. Oh, he was Butler. Yeah.
Yeah.
That's why he had a number that he used to play with brass band. Yeah. He tried 16th and written on March. Uh-huh.

This past the street is right on the old mountain. Somebody, uh, Bunk told me it was second and magazine, they used to call it, where he was a butler. I think his wife told us that too, Mrs. Stella Oliver. Yeah. What do you want to see? Magazine Street, I believe, I'm not sure, you know.

He used to come on a Saturday night. Uh-huh. In that time, they had the Eagle band. Yeah. He used to come on Saturday night. Yeah. And treat the band. I told y'all, Frank, I didn't play a 16-Ribbon March. Uh-huh. And he got out on his feet. I wondered when you first played with Joe then, you wouldn't play the dance the first
you said panel. No, no. Did you play with him then later?

Uh, later then I went with him, yes. After he got so he could play the dance music then, he could read, wonderful reader with one eye. He had a glass eye, but he was a wonderful sight reader. But he couldn't play much at that time. He couldn't play no head music, you know. All he could read. Then after he picked up that dance music, well then he was able to play without the music. And he just went right on up and got with, after him and Louis Armstrong got together, and they doubled up and went left here and went away.
And you remember who else was in the band with Oliver when you worked with him and where

you played? Uh, let's see now. We played so many different, we was playing spot job. We didn't have no sound plays until we went to Hunson Nagel. Now, uh, let's see. What color was this, Hunson Nagel? He had, uh, Liberty in the Outerville. Liberty. He's band, he had, uh, uh, Call it the Casino. Oh yeah. He had, uh, Chris Kelly. Uh, no, uh, he had, uh, uh, Chris Miner on the drum. And he had, uh, uh, Alphonse Piku. And, uh, Joe Atkins. Uh, Joe Atkins. Uh. Joe Atkins. Uh. Joe Atkins. Ed Atkins. Ed Atkins was, yeah. On trombone that one. Yeah, on trombone. I was playing guitar. He had, uh, he had, uh, Pop Foster on the bass. Uh, he had Pop Foster's brother Willie Foster on the violin. That's it.
That was the Magnolia band. Do you remember, uh, I think, uh, Louie Kepard tells me that he played in the Magnolia band too with Oliver for a while.
He played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played a little while, yeah. But he didn't play long. He ain't, he wasn't much of him. He played a little while.
Uh huh. And you played guitar then, but that was before Louie Kepard then, you joined him.
Yeah. Uh huh.
Uh, did you play any later jobs, any place much in the district with Joe or other places?
No, the only place where I played them was right down in Ponsonagle then. Uh huh.
At the casino. Was that sort of a cabaret, what was it, uh, or? The dance hall. It was the dance hall. It was the local dance hall. And dance hall and dance hall. Hmm.

And it was the casino dance hall, but it ran by Hunts. Hunts, uh, and Eddie Groeschel. Yeah, that's right. And they called it Hunts and Nagels. Yeah, that's right. Hunts and Nagels. Hunts and Nagels, they called it like that. Yeah. Through Hunts. Yeah, that's right. And Eddie Groeschel. Eddie Groeschel was his partner. It was his partnership. He was a partnership. But the name of it was the casino. Yeah, that's the casino.
Yeah. The other night also we were talking about Sidney Bechet.
Oh, yeah. He told that funny story about him being on the Smoky Mary. Tell us about it.

We used to play at Millenburg for picnics out there. Those were only picnics. And Sidney Bechet, he was playing clarinet with us, you see. And well, and Manuel Perez was playing trumpet. And we had the same fella Jimmy Pollard playing violin too. He used to play with his two over there. And we'd play them picnics. Cause we used to take a man when needed a man on the picnic. We'd have extra man when needed, you see. And Sidney Bechet would get on that old Smoky Mary, you know, that running out the Millenburg and that we'd be short of waiting for him. And we couldn't find, we didn't know the trouble. They'd send me out there to look to the train and see if I could locate him. Well, I'd go out there and I'd look on the train. I asked the conductor, I'd say, if you've seen a musician lately on this train, he said, the fella there back in the coach, they had been on there and made three trips. And he's got some kind of little box there that was his clarinet. Well, I'd go there and wake him up, you know, and bring him over to the saloon and wash his face and give him a glass of wine. And revive him up and come on back there and play the picnic. How'd he play in those days? Oh, he used to play, I'll tell you. Well, we had a regular Dixieland band too, you know. You know, we could play classic music too. That was Jim and Paul had nothing but the music. Emanuel Peres said he didn't carry nothing but the strictness music. Almost all the men in the band could read good. But they could play that Dixieland too.
Well, speaking of that term Dixieland, I never did ask fast either. When the word jazz began being used here in New Orleans, can you remember?
That was used right around Basin Street when we was playing. We started around by Harry Parker. And yes, Harry Parker, that's when we started that Dixieland.
I mean, that word, they called the jazz band. Was that the first time you ever heard of it? Oh, yes.
That's the way it started from, right around Basin in Ivorville. All around that, well, it was the district at that time. All around, through and there, you see.
Can you remember the first time you heard that word fast when they called anything a jazz band rather than a ragtime band or whatever they called it?

No, I remember it was very round, round the district like you said. That's a lot. Mm-hmm. And Dixieland came. Dixieland came on. Well, the district was born. The band was uptown. Field, a lot of bands up in the field.
And then they called that Dixieland.
Mm-hmm. Dixieland.
Have they used that word jazz any place else before? Do you know? No. Or how they come to call it a jazz band, have you any idea? They called it Dixieland.
Yeah, they called it Dixieland.

Yeah, they just would, you know, different bands would name what they want to their band. Say like Joe Oliver had a band, you'd say Joe Oliver's Dixieland band or some other band would say Joe Galloway. Galloway's Ragtime band and all that.

Well, that used to be the old bands. Mm-hmm. The old bands out in the field, uptown. Yeah. The Ragtime. Ragtime band. I called that Ragtime band, like Buddy Bowling. Yeah, like Buddy Bowling. Olivier, Charlie Galloway.
Yeah, Charlie Galloway. Yeah.

The Olivia band, I called it Olivier. Well, they had several other bands. Johnny Brown, here. Yeah, that's right. Well, that was Ragtime band. They called it Frank's band Ragtime band. Yeah. They joined in from Ragtime, to the Dixieland. Yeah.
And that Pelican band from uptown there, what you call them, playing trumpet there, Eddie, and they had a, what's the name, uh, it was Frankie Duesen. Frankie Duesen.

Oh, yeah. Well, that was the town, that was, uh, that was Ragtime band. Yeah. That was Ragtime band. They had the Frank's, ah, alright. I think that was a good one. That's when Frank takes the band, and he left John Pendleton, well, John Pendleton, you know, he could play a kind of style of music. No. Well, I had another fella. His name was Ned. Yeah. Yeah. That's Terry's band, but men like to travel around, so he went away. See, Frank's taken up on Edwark Clem.

Edwark Clem, well, that's the one I was talking about on the trumpet, Edwark Clem. Oh, yeah. He was another fella that had one eye, too. He used to wear black glasses all the time. You couldn't tell it. My glasses are such an app. Yeah. But he was a good trumpet player, though. Oh, yeah.
He was all there, though.
Yeah. Yeah, Joe Welch was playing drums. Oh, Joe Welch? Yeah. Joe Welch played drums.
I was going to ask a bit more about Galloway. Charlie Galloway, was that his name?
That was his name, and that was his band. He was a one-legged man, and he played bass. What did he used to call him the Lovin' Galloway?
Lovin' Galloway.
He played bass violin. Seems like somebody once called him Happy Galloway. Yes, that's right.
Happy Galloway, that's right.
Happy Galloway and the Lovin' people. People used to call him Lovin' Galloway. You know, they have a time, they Lovin' different names. Lovin' Galloway, you know.

You say he was a one-legged man? One leg, yeah. He had a stick. He had a stick, a kind of a crutch, you know. He used to support his stuff with that bad leg, you know. And he could carry that bass. Them times you carry the bass on your back with a strap, you see. Yeah. He could really get around with it.
What style did he play? Did he use the bow or did he use the bow? Oh, the bow.
When the bows.
Oh, yes. Them times, that's all.
Only time they pick is when the band's going out of the last chorus.
That's right. A good bow. Do you remember, Sir Dorsey, the first time you heard anybody pick on the bass? Well, I was the first one started that, right down in the district.

I started Pop Foster, and he'll tell you he's living the day. I started with that one finger, picking that four-four rhythm. And from that on, they start making that four-four rhythm, you know, picking with one finger like that. You put the bow down. And they just went right on up. And when I looked around there, all the bass players was playing that four-four rhythm. Then they was making that vancing all the time, you see. They got so they was playing with three fingers and stuff.
And you remember some of the other bass players you've mentioned, three or four. Any of the other fellas real early that you heard?

No, not the old fellas, no. Do you remember Jimmy Johnson? Jimmy Johnson. Was he older than you, I guess? Oh, yes, yes. He was older than me, yes. He died. He was a good bass player, yes. And Jimmy Johnson. I love him. And Jimmy Brown, too, was another bass player. He was the greatest one. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
You were talking about Sidney Maché going to the street there, going back?

Yeah, and they'd send me out there to go catch the train when it'd blow, it'd blow, you know. We'd be well over there in the camp. All the men, we done played a couple of numbers already waiting. I'd go out there and ask the conductor and fix him to go back and sit. I'd say, you seen a fellow musician? There's a fellow up there in the seat there, he'd been sleeping. We'd brought him back to town about three times. He'd go back there and say, get up here, bitch, get up. Pull him up, get his horn, and bring him outside and bring him to one of them ballrooms right across from, you know, and make him wash his face, you know, straighten up, get him a wine, and give him a fresh wine, and he'd come on back out to that picnic, that camp, and blow that thing. I mean, he could blow.
Really good then, he was pretty young then, I guess.
Yes, indeed, he could play. He looked like nothing wouldn't happen to him, but he just like that. Yes, sir.
Now, the other day you were playing with Peter Bocard there. Is that the first time you worked with Peter?

No, no, I worked with Pete for a long time. He played, I played practically, just like I said, Pete would play from different bands, with one band from another, see, but he played, he played most of that with that tuxedo band, you know, and the Eureka, he played with all them bands, different bands, and now, because he just, he just made this band up, this band, what he's got now, he called it the Creole Serenators. Oh yeah, that's the late years. Yeah, that's the late years, the Creole Serenators, you see, and that's his own band, but he never did have no band of his own a long time ago. He used to be in different bands, you know. What did he play, violin? He played violin, yeah. That was his only instrument, violin. He never knew nothing about no trumpet, until the late days, you know, going by, he started playing trumpet, but that was his first instrument, violin.
Was the violin always the leader of the band?

Yeah. Well, it's a leading instrument, but any man that's got the job, you know, handling the band, running the band, you know, managing the band, he's supposed to be the leader, you see. Well, who does the stomping of? Well, the trumpet player. The trumpet player? Yeah, he's supposed to be the leader, you know, the...
And if you haven't got a trumpet?

A clarinet or sax or something like that, you know, any leading instrument. It could be the violin. The violin, the violin could, the violin is a leading instrument too, yeah, it's a leading instrument. But you take a heavy band, and it's more better for one of the brass or the reed to lead, you know. The violin is soft, you know. It fills in.
Did you ever play with Celestan or Emma Barrett?
I played a couple of jobs with Papa, but not to be in the band, you know, not regular, no. Did you ever work with Emma Barrett much? Emma? Sure, I worked with Emma a good many times.
I was thinking you'd work with her soon.

I worked with her a good many times, yeah. I think I worked with her originally. And that before carnival, I think it was during the carnival season, gone. I worked at Brennan's, up here on the... Yeah, I worked there. She was at the absent house. Yeah. She lost, I think she lost out there. Yeah, she's not there anymore now. She had that job, you see.
I just wondered in the old days, a long time ago, 30 years or so ago, if you ever played with her. She used to be with Celestan or Emma Barrett.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Did you ever work with the old man, the gentleman, Robichaud?
Yeah, I played a while with him. He played guitar with him when he was playing at the Lyric, at the Lyric Theater.
You were at the Lyric Ender a while?
Yeah, yeah, Lyric.
Played bass there?
No, guitar. Guitar. You see, he's had a... His first guitar player he had was... was... Coochie Morton.
I've heard of him.

His brother was a drummer, wasn't he? Yeah, yeah. Henry Morton. Henry Morton. After he got... After Coochie Morton... Coochie Morton stayed with him a long time. Then, after Coochie Morton left, fell out or something, broke away from him. Then I came in behind Coochie Morton and I played a while. I didn't play long. And right after I left, he got Bud Scott.
Oh yeah. I knew Bud Scott.

Bud Scott on the guitar. And Bud Scott stayed with him practically until his band broke up. The Robichaud was a left-handed violin player. Old John Robichaud. And he had... He had two Kimballs in his band, you know. He had one called Henry Kimball, that was his bass player. And Andrew Kimball. The trumpet player. Andrew Kimball and Henry Kimball. And Henry Kimball is still active playing now. He plays baseball and he's a... He's a... a... a...
a... a... Yeah. Well, I've been trying to think for three days of a trumpet player. I told Ralph the other day, it begins with K. from uptown. It went through my head. Keelan. Frank Keelan?

Frank Keelan was a trumpet player. With this one of these old... You know, like you ever heard him, I guess you would call it a barrel house. You know. That's a barrel house. That's a barrel house. That's a barrel house. Yeah. Well, he didn't play in all these good time, big time bands, you know. But all those bands like we were like... I had one time when we was playing up at Tom Anderson. When I worked at Tom Anderson, he played... He played trumpet in there, because he... It was... He played soft trumpet, you know. He didn't play that heavy loud like these...
He wasn't so loud then.

No, he wasn't too loud, but he could play good though. Yeah. And... Well, then they used... At Tom Anderson, they used two guitars, you see. Because they had more vocal. The fellas... There were two men in the band. Snow and this other fella, Charlie Washington. Them two fellas could sing. And this other fella, Tom Brown, who played the mandolin. He could play mandolin by note. But he read music. Yeah. Well, he was the leader. And then I played bass, you know. I'd taken Sam Orange's place on the bass. And I played... Then they hired Frank Keelan. Frank Keelan played trumpet. And then after Frank, he liked his liquor too, you know. And he got so he couldn't... Half the time he wouldn't show up. Then he got... This fella from way uptown, I forget his name. Played vowel trombone. He had a barbershop way up there. That's his name, you know.
It wasn't carnish.
It wasn't carnish.
Cornish?
Cornish? No, no. It wasn't cornish. Where? Oh, I can't think of that fella's name. He died. He was a good vowel trombone player.
Then Dutre...
No, no. Dutre played a slide trombone.
Yeah. Who came later?
Sam Dutre and Nora Dutre.
Yeah. You ever worked much with the Dutres? Their son is in the town. That is Sam's son is in town out there on Bourbon Street. We saw him last night.
Yeah.
His son? Yeah. Young Sam came out at Appaloosa. He lived up there.

I don't know much about him. But I know Nora Dutre and Sam and... Yeah, I know them. I played with them, you know, many times. Yeah. Nora and Sam. I don't know. Let's see. Did you hear anything else about Tom Anderson's? When were you there about... That's...
That was around... That was around 1905. That really? Yeah, around 1905.
Yeah, that was around 1905.
Yeah, that was around 1905.
Yeah, that was around 1905. Yeah, that was around 1905. You started on bass then? You said that you wanted to play bass? I could play... I could play...
Well, I wasn't too much of a bass player, but I could, you know...

You were starting on that. Yeah, starting, yeah. Little place like that entertaining band, you know, as long as you could make a couple of notes on it, you could make out, you see. And that's where I practically started. Now, they had that entertaining band. Now, they didn't have... The only time they got Frank Keelan is when after they started getting the horns and, you know...
After Kevron all started getting the horns.

Yeah, yeah. Then they... Well, frankly, old Tom Anderson can do anything he want in the city because he was a big... He was a big boss. Yeah, he was a big boss in the city, yeah. Anything he... When they would go around raiding any place, they never bought his place. No one did, not Tom Anderson. And he was... He kept his band all the time. He had two places. He had one on Basin and... And... Yeah, and Iverville. And he had one on Ramport between Canal and Iverville.
Which one did you play in there?

I practically played both sides of the... Yeah, I played both of them. Because you see on the other side on Ramport Street, every time... Every birthday he had, he celebrated birthday. Right. And he'd get the band in there. Yeah. Yeah. To have a big time. That old man... He was an old man, but he just was spoke. He had plenty of money too. He was rich. Yeah. Get a crowd of women and everything in there and have his band and note and champagne and stuff. We'd have a time back up in there.
Was he married to Gertrude Dix? Do you remember? And one of the... We had one of the houses and the madam went next door. Do you remember? Who? Was Tom Anderson married to Gertrude Dix?
Oh, no.
She was one of the land ladies and all that.
I don't... I never did know that.
Seems like I heard that. I don't know that. His wife is supposed to be living that today. Yeah? Yeah. She lives in the fence border on Bourbon Street, I believe.

Well, he had so many women around his place all the time. I didn't know one from the other, you know. I never did know his wife, you know. Much as I played around there for him. Because he was well liked by the women folks, you know. Of course, he was a big sports, you know. And he had all kind of fine women there in his place.
Did he have rooms upstairs for them?

Yeah, I think he had upstairs. He had a nice place there on Ramport Street there. Is that the one they call the annex? Yeah, I believe it is. Between Canal and... You'll see. On this corner there was mush... Not mush there. Uh... Uh... Uh... Uh... Funniture store. Oh. That's that old furniture store there was there. Uh... Uh... Name after that old mayor... Maestry? Maestry. Maestry's furniture store was there. Mike Maestry and his dad, about three or four brothers. Uh-huh. Had the furniture store right at the corner. On Ivor Village.
I've seen a picture of that place.

Yeah. Now he had waiters, colored waiters, you know, in both of them places, you see. On Ramport and they had colored waiters over on either, on the base of them. Yeah. Well that was most of the bar room there. Big bar room he had at that corner, you see. Yeah. And they had what uh say like wine rooms, you know, in the back. You know, had little boots, you see, for private people to go in and sit for the curtains like that. But we'd sit in the back on the corner and entertain, you know. Then Tom Brown would open one other side of the door and we'd sing and play and the people coming in the bar would come and throw money in the kiddie box, you see. You know, we made good money there. So, had really good times there. So, uh, that's where Frank Keeling come around. He, but he, now he'd fill in on them little uh, light jobs, you know, like that way, like little fish fries and things like that, you know, to play. But he was so on the line half of the time, he couldn't depend on him, you know. A fella like him and get a couple of drinks in him, you know, and he might not show up, you see. But he was alright though, he could play. He played good.
Are there any other bands there on your list that we neglected to ask about?
Uh, I'm Anderson, Harry Parker's name. I'll tell you about Harry Parker's name.
What was your first job, Eddie? Do you remember?

Uh, let's see, I, I couldn't, let me first job, let's see. Oh yeah, first job, I'll tell you my first job. Our first job was with Kenneas Jackson. I played guitar. I was working at Thompson Sawmill. Where was that? Broad and Portis. I was working, working at Thompson Sawmill and I could play guitar, you know. I, I'll tell you how I played guitar. I wasn't, say, complimenting, you know, I could just, could pick the guitar, you know. And that time you'd pick it, pick it with your finger, you know, put a strap around your neck. And I'd go all around that, that, the, the, the battlefield they call it that, around there. Well, them people used to give fish fries around there, you see. On Saturday night, they'd give them fish fries. And I used to make money too, you know, cause they'd, uh, well if I got a dollar and a half, a dollar, two dollars a night, I was doing good. And, uh, they'd sell, put the red light out on the gate and, and, and, and fish fries, you know. And I'd play, play the guitar for them and had the harmonica with the rack around it and blow the harmonica and play the guitar, you see. And I was the one man band. Well, I'd sit on the chair there, they'd give me all I want to drink and they'd pay me off too after the fish. Well, that's where I, now I'll tell you how I started. Now that's how I started. Well, Kenneas found out I could play, I was a good guitar player. Well, he had a, uh, a job down here in Rice's place. Rice, that was sort of a beer parlor down in the district too. At Marais, at, uh, at, uh, not Marais, let's see.
You see, Pete Lala was on Marais street.
You know, Marais, well you see where, uh, uh, uh, uh, where Pete Lala was on this side? Yeah, I know that's where. Along the other side.
Right across the street.

Yeah, yeah. Well, that's where Kenneas had it now. He was a violin player. He used to take cigarette, smoke cigarette and stick it behind his ear, you know, like that, and keep it lit, you see. And played violin. Nothing but soft music, you see. Yeah. Violin, guitar, bass, like that, you see. And, uh, so he hired me to play with him that night. Down at Rice, that's where I started with the guitar. And I think we made about 23 or 24 dollars a piece that night. I wasn't getting but nine dollars a week out to the lumber yard. And he told me that was a regular job for me every night. So I'd have said, well, that kind of money, I was, goodbye lumber yard. And I stayed there a long time, you know, around there, that place there. How old would you be about then?
You'd be quite young then, would you?
Well, uh, I think I was around, must have been around about 22, 23 years old. Oh yeah, he was old.

Oh, I see, Fess was talking about someplace, McNicious place. What was that, the fellow ran and had a bar, was that at that corner too? Hmm. Remember the name right now? Yeah. McNicious or something like that. Hmm. McNicious, yeah, I remember McNicious. There was a place there, but I don't remember how hard it was.

The only ones I know, and I practically know that place, from around there, from Iverville, the Rays all the way up to Ramport Street. Iverville, Bienville, I don't know no McNicious place, the only thing. Lala, I know Pete Lala, there was, like I told you, Lala was on the Rays in Iverville.
Remember dance hall, Abadeez or something, did they have music in the saloon? Abadeez. Abadeez. Abadeez. Abadeez.
Abadeez. That name sounds muted, but I can't place where it was.

Oh, here's something I want to ask you, Eddie. I noticed where 25s used to be, before they laid the new sidewalk there, they had a name in the sidewalk, J-N-O-T Lala, outside the big 25s there. Was that his name, the man that ran 25s? J-N-O-T Lala. Yes, J-N-O-T Lala. I think the first called him J-N-O-T Lala.
Well, they had a couple of brothers of them Lala. J-N-O-T Lala, Pete Lala. I practically didn't know their names too good, you know.
Do you think one of the Lalas ran 25s at one time?

I don't remember. No. I used to bum around there all the time, but I never knew who owned the place and who run it. I know the bartender called Henry Bowser, which used to be bartending around there in that time, you know, big brown-skinned fella. Henry Bowser? J-Henry Bowser. Bowser. Bowser, yeah. He was bartending at that time around there. When me and Mineta was playing at Parkish Place there, 101.
Did they have a place to dance in 25s? No.
They just had a gambling place there. Gambling room. Yeah, they had a gambling place in the back. They had a ball on the sides, you know.

Any piano or any other instrument in there? No. Somebody called us once Joe Oliver might have worked there and had his band. Did you remember? At 25? Yeah, they remember Joe Oliver playing there at the band.

No. Unless he played, sometimes the fellas would go and play like that for a date or, you know. That's something special. Special or something. Special or something. But I didn't know no place for the dance there. I know. That's my time. I know they had, they used to play, have big gambling places back there, you see. They had gambling too, big coach games and everything back there. What is that coach? This is almost like a five-up game, but it's a different deal, different cards, you know. Oh, it's a card game? Yeah, it's a card game. You bet, you know, the fellas got the biggest hand. Oh, yeah. And then, yeah. Three cards, you say? No, five cards. Five cards. Yeah, yeah. You get them face down? Yeah, face down, yeah. And you bet without looking? Well, no, you look at your hand first, you see. And if you see if you got, it's like that, and a three-six, it's a big hand, you know. And so they can tell how many cards they want to draw, you see, how many cards they want to hold, you see. Oh, yeah. And if they see where they're taking a chance, the two cards they're holding, if they got two sixes they're holding, they might take and discard the tree and draw three cards and figure they might catch another six, you see. Almost like a poker game. Yeah, yeah. Almost like a draw poker. Yeah. And sometimes all the fellas got the biggest hand, just win the pot, you see.
Do they still play country around here?

Yeah, but it ain't much, too. No, it ain't, no. They don't play it for big money like they used to. No. No, they have little penny-hand games, you know, just passing time, that's all. The biggest games going on now is the poker game, no? Yeah. Yeah, that's big money games, them poker games, only plays. And these houses have them great big poker games and there's plenty of money to be made off that poker, the cutting, you see, the cuts every, they cut so much on that game, you see. And win, too, you can win, too. You got some smart poker players, you can win plenty of money on it. You got women playing that now. Yeah? Yeah, indeed. You got women playing that poker. But it ain't why, it's kind of dangerous now on account of the law, you see. They read them all the time. They read, yes. They have to be careful now where they have, where they have in that.
Did women play gamble much in the old days?
Oh, yeah, they always did gamble, you know. They always, women always did gamble, shoot dice and everything else.
I was going to ask about some other places in the district, the Tuxedo Dance Hall. Did you ever play there? Tuxedo?
Tuxedo.
Across the street from the entertainers on Franklin Street. Was that Billy Phillips? Billy Phillips.

Place? Billy Phillips. Billy Phillips. Billy Phillips on, on, on, that was on, on Franklin. Yeah, between Ivville and Bimble on the left-hand side. Yeah. Yeah, he had a place there, too, yeah. But he didn't have much of a dancing place there, you know. Like a hall and a ball. And they had two entrances, see. One entrance around on, on, on, on, uh, uh, Liberty Street. Isn't that Liberty? Uh, let's see, there's Franklin. And, yeah, Liberty. Liberty. Liberty. They had, they had a sort of an alley. Yeah. Liberty. Yeah. Liberty. You can come through that alley and go right on back in to the ball. They had a music stand, built on side the wall. And, uh, he'd have a band to play there, you see. And, uh, mostly entertainment and, uh, women folks and all, in the front, they had a sort of a, uh, patio on that side. Yeah. And, uh, they'd all sit around the tables and drink, most of the entertainment, you know. Now and then they'd get up and jump up there and get, you know, chances and go in and around it. So, we, and, uh, that was Billy Phillip. And, uh, he had, uh, he had that place that, he had a place up in, in the Tender Line, round, round, round, round, Howard and, uh, uh, uh, Grabby.
Uptown in there, too.
Yeah, they had a place there, right at the corner. They had a big boy there.
I didn't know that. Mm-hmm.
Uh, they had a big fella they called George Jones, used to play.
Oh, a bass player, was it? Yeah. Yeah, I remember that. And they also used to keep all the hips or something, didn't they? You'd grab all the hips.

That string band, like he said, he had a string band, you see. He could sing, and he'd hire a good violin player, you see. And he'd hire a fella like me on a guitar, a good guitar player. And he'd take his bass while, he wasn't, he was no kind of bass player, he just tuned, half of the time he wasn't even tuned up. Just any kind of way you know.
I think Johnny St. Cyr said he used to use ropes.

Yeah, he used to take, uh, he'd break a string, you know, one of his, uh, string. He'd get an old sash cord and put it on there. And they could rouse him, and rouse him up and put it on there and wind up, go on, let's go. And, you don't tell him you ain't tuned, just let him go, but he's a money getter though. Yeah. Yeah, you see, he could take and, uh, see you'd have a bunch of men, and, uh, he was well-liked. And he'd get a, he could rhyme. See, like you named Mr. Russell, somebody, meet him in the back and tell him that man in there, the name is Mr. Russell. He's in the shoe business, or he's in such and such a business. And he'd come on in and start to sing and play and rhyme on you, and make all kind of rhymes on you. Then, then you would know how you got your name, you see. Johnny St. Cyr, talking about the same thing. Somebody in the gang had done told him, you know, that your name. Well, quite naturally, after he rhymed so good on you, you'd get your wallet off when you get through it and give him a $5, $10 bill, something like that. Well, he was good. But, before I was playing the bass, he couldn't, he had an old rag cracked up bass. He didn't care to throw it around any kind of way. And I went all the way to Indianapolis, Indiana with him.
Yeah, yeah.

Went with the shrines. I went to Indianapolis with him. I took my tenor banjo that, uh, when I, when I went up there, there people were surprised. They had never seen him, had never seen a tenor banjo up there before. Yeah? Oh. And, uh, I, uh, he had, he had this, this fellow called Snow on the guitar, and Jim Dixon, and myself, and Cornelius, that same fellow I told you, with, uh, had a cigarette you put behind his head. And, and the shrines, uh, the shrines hired him. He got, he got us. I was on my vacation. I was working at the bank, and I, I was on my vacation. And, uh, he taken, and, uh, they gave us, uh, them, you know how they, how they, how they, oh, uh, them farmers wear them, uh, overhaul pants. Yeah. And blue, uh, jumpers, you know, jumpers and red handkerchief. Yeah, like that. Around the neck, you see, and them big old sun hats. And they had a couple of big bales of cotton, you see, on the float. And we got to Memphis, we parade all around in Memphis, you see. When we sitting up on the bale of cotton, he was singing, he could sing all them old, old-time songs, you know, like honeysuckle and all that, man. And, uh, we parade all around Memphis, and then we come all back and got in the train, and went all the way to Indianapolis, you see. At, uh, the Panama Limit was the train that went off, and them shrines, all them nobles were in the shrines. They had, uh, I see, I think, uh, uh, this fella, the wine boy, he was portentated at the shrine. Well, they had a carload, nothing, nothing, nothing but liquor in the back. They had a big camel in the back, and they brought the camel and all, and they had, uh, that, that place over there was dry. Indiana was dry. Yeah, they brought their own liquor. And, uh, we just pulled all, it was just like Carnival over there. And as soon as we made the parade in, uh, on Main Street, uh, by the Claypool Hotel, and a girl was way up in one of the hotel windows, she fell out and went and killed herself. Leaned too far over. Yeah. Yeah, it was a first accident in the parade. And we, uh, we paraded all around in Indianapolis, and, uh, and then we went downstairs, they went up, up in, uh, I think about 23 stories high, the Claypool Hotel is. And they went up in, uh, special room up there, and they had the Archbishop, the Bishop was up there with them, you know. The shrine was strong, you know. And, uh, we, uh, down in the basement down there playing on one side we was playing on, and on the other side the Highway and Band was playing on the other side. We had two bands. Ah, we were banding on one side, we were on the other side. Oh, we made plenty money. Uh-huh. We, we, we left here on a Sunday, and we can get back to, like, Friday night. Oh.
And they paid, uh, your way and all your expenses? Oh, yeah, sure. Yeah.
Yeah. Everything's playing.
So, everything. And then, you say they've never seen a tenor banjo on there.

No, they never saw a tenor banjo. About what year that was? Oh, let's see. Oh, you got me now. Uh, 17, 19, 17, 19, 18. The time of the First World War, you think? 19, it was right after that, uh, uh, about 1919. Oh, yeah. About 1919, that was. Oh, yeah. Because I, I went, I went to the Whitney in 1917. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Are you still mad by the way?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. All this time, right? Yeah.
Still mad. Right, yeah. Right, yeah.
42 years. That's wonderful.
Mm-hmm. When Johnny St. Cyr said Balto used to play with John sometimes and violinists. Oh, yeah, Valto.
Valto. Oh, yeah. He was a good violin player. A Creole fellow, Valto. Yeah, he was good. Who was, he was one of the very best?
Who was the best violinist and violinist you heard?

I think, to my, to my idea, I think, uh, uh, I believe, uh, uh, uh, Jim Apala, I think Jim Apala was about the best violin, violin player. And, uh, well, Peter Bocos, he, he was good. I think, now let's see, uh, uh, after, after Jim Apala, I think Peter Bocos came second. Now, Manu Mineta used to play violin too. That's right.
He was a good violin player too.

I'm telling you, Manu Mineta could play a good violin. And he, I think, uh, now I say, I'll say it like this. Jim Apala was the leader. Say, Manu Mineta came second. Then Peter Bocos behind him. I think that, I rate him like that. Yeah. Then, then after the hat, after that come, uh, come, uh, uh, Valto. And after Valto come Tinette. Now Tinette was, uh, Tinette was a violin player too. He was good. Uh-huh. Yeah. You heard of him? I don't remember that, man. No, Tinette, yeah. Well, that's the, that's the one. Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Opening: name and introduction
segments.summary: Russell asks Dawson for his name (Eddie Joseph Dawson) and begins the questions.

segments.title: Dawson's list of bands and dance halls, 1904 onward
segments.summary: Dawson reads off his career: dance halls and bandleaders from 1904 (Parker's, Anderson's, Phillips', Oliver, Kelly, Rene); with Manetta he corrects the dates for Puclos and Parker's.

segments.title: The first band at Puclos
segments.summary: The O'Neil Lavish band at Puclos was a small group of five: violin, piano, tenor banjo, saxophone and trumpet.

segments.title: Birth, family and first instrument
segments.summary: Born July 24 (1884); no musicians in the family; he picked up the guitar by himself at about 19 or 20.

segments.title: Photographs of Kid Clayton and his Happy Pals
segments.summary: Looking at photos of Kid Clayton's Happy Pals; identifying the drummer and the private uptown dance where it was taken.

segments.title: Bands heard as a boy: Blaze Away, Galloway, Silver Leaf
segments.summary: Uptown dance bands and lawn parties he heard before playing; Silver Leaf, Bunk Johnson, Humphrey, and the Billy Phillips fire.

segments.title: Guitar lessons and learning from Fess Manetta
segments.summary: A white visitor gave him four guitar lessons; Manetta helped; he moved to tenor banjo after six or seven years of guitar.

segments.title: Playing guitar with John Robichaux at the Lyric Theater
segments.summary: He played guitar with Robichaux's band at the Lyric before the First World War, before Bud Scott took over; the Lyric dated to about 1908.

segments.title: Taking up string bass and tenor banjo
segments.summary: Hired as bass player by Manuel Perez's Imperial band after Billy Moran left; self-taught on bass, about ten years on tenor banjo.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and the Magnolia band
segments.title: Freddie Keppard and the trumpet at Huntson Nagel's
segments.summary: The 101 Ranch band was strings only; brass was illegal in the District until Keppard played and Parker got a permit, creating the Magnolia band.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and the Magnolia band
segments.title: Early lineups with Manetta, Palao and the clarinetists
segments.summary: Dawson and Manetta recall the string band's personnel: Black Pete, Palao, Joe Nicholas and George Baquet.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and the Magnolia band
segments.title: Joe Oliver learning dance music
segments.summary: Oliver first could only play brass band music; Dawson hired a substitute for a dance; Oliver later became a fine sight reader and left with Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Keppard, Oliver and the Magnolia band
segments.title: The Magnolia band at Huntson Nagel's Casino
segments.summary: Personnel of Oliver's Magnolia band at the Casino dance hall, Louis Keppard's brief stay, and the Hunts and Nagel ownership.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet asleep on the Smoky Mary
segments.summary: Dawson tells how he fetched a sleeping young Bechet from the train to Milneburg picnics, with Perez and Palao in the band.

segments.title: When the word jazz and Dixieland came into use
segments.summary: Dawson and Manetta recall that bands around Basin Street were called Dixieland, with uptown ragtime bands before.

segments.title: Pelican band and the trumpeters Dusen and Clem
segments.summary: Recollections of the Pelican band, Frankie Dusen, John Pendleton and a one-eyed trumpeter.

segments.title: Charlie Galloway, the one-legged bass player
segments.summary: Galloway played bowed bass with a crutch, known as Happy or Lovin' Galloway.

segments.title: Dawson's claim to start picking the bass; other early bassists
segments.summary: Dawson says he started four-four finger picking, which Pop Foster and others followed; remembers Jimmy Johnson and Jimmy Brown.

segments.title: Bechet on the Smoky Mary, continued
segments.summary: Dawson repeats how he fetched sleeping Bechet from the train and sobered him up for the picnic; Bechet could really play.

segments.title: Peter Bocage and who leads a band
segments.summary: Dawson on Bocage's bands and violin, and on whether the trumpet or violin should lead.

segments.title: Working with Celestin and Emma Barrett
segments.summary: A few jobs with Celestin and many with Emma Barrett, including Brennan's.

segments.title: Guitarists under Robichaux and the Kimball brothers
segments.summary: Coochie Morton, Dawson and Bud Scott as guitarists with Robichaux; Henry and Andrew Kimball.

segments.title: Frank Keelan and the entertaining band at Tom Anderson's
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Tom Anderson's band in 1905 with two guitars, Tom Brown, Frank Keelan, and the Dutreys.

segments.title: Tom Anderson's two places and the band's role
segments.summary: Anderson's places on Basin Street and Rampart; his influence, birthday parties and money, and the singing waiters.

segments.title: Dawson's first job at Rice's with Kenneas Jackson
segments.summary: He played fish fries as a one-man band, then Jackson hired him at Rice's across from Pete Lala's, paying far above his sawmill wage.

segments.title: Pete Lala, the 25s and its gambling room
segments.summary: Questions about McNicious, Lala's and the 25s: gambling, the bartender Henry Bowser, whether Oliver played there.

segments.title: Coosh games, poker and women gamblers
segments.summary: Dawson explains the card game, how poker now is the big money game, and that women always gambled.

segments.chapter: Billy Phillips, George Jones and the Shriners trip
segments.title: Billy Phillips' dance hall and George Jones
segments.summary: Description of the Tuxedo/Billy Phillips hall on Franklin Street and Phillips' place uptown run by George Jones.

segments.chapter: Billy Phillips, George Jones and the Shriners trip
segments.title: George Jones as the rhyming bass player
segments.summary: Jones's string band, bass tied with sash cord, and his rhymes on customers for tips.

segments.chapter: Billy Phillips, George Jones and the Shriners trip
segments.title: The Shriners trip to Indianapolis
segments.summary: Dawson went with Jones's band to Indianapolis via Memphis in costume, expenses paid, with his tenor banjo a novelty there.

segments.title: Ranking the New Orleans violinists
segments.summary: Dawson ranks Palao first, Manetta, Bocage, Valto and Tinette next.
